newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says closely watching Syrian-Iran ties.
newsitem.headline: Israel says closely watching Syrian-Iran ties.

text.p: Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said on Monday a rare visit by Syrian President Hafez al-Assad to Iran was "not a good sign" and Israel was watching closely to see if two of its staunchest foes were closing ranks.

"President Assad's visit to Iran...after many, many years during which he did not visit Iran, is not a good sign. We will continue to follow this closening (in ties) and if we must we will take steps," Mordechai said.
Mordechai did not specify what action Israel might take, but he said it had no aggressive intent on any states in the region.

Assad used his trip to Tehran on Thursday, only his second to Iran since its 1979 Islamic revolution, to shore up Iranian support for his demand Israel withdraw from the Golan Heights, the strategic Syrian plateau it occupied in 1967.

Syria and Iran called jointly for an end to Israeli occupation of all Arab land and voiced support for Hizbollah (Party of God) guerrillas fighting to oust Israeli troops from a south Lebanon occupation zone.
The two allies also urged Moslem Turkey to stop its growing military cooperation with the Jewish state.
"(Syria) is certainly worried by the process of closening between us and the Turks," Mordechai told reporters after a parliamentary foreign affairs and defence committee meeting.
"We are assisting Turkey in certain military fields but have no intentions to take any steps against any state...in the Middle East or elsewhere," he said.

Israel and Syria have failed in five years of sporadic peace talks to agree on the fate of the Golan. Talks were suspended shortly before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took office last year.
Netanyahu's opposition to the principle of trading captured Arab land for peace appeared to close off prospects of fresh talks.
Iran says Israel has no right to exist and Tehran has been vehemently opposed to the Middle East peace process.
The Itim news agency quoted Mordechai as saying Iran was not able to launch a missile strike on Israel.
"But they are working to acquire them, including non-conventional (weapons)" he added.
